items.title: Logging In to Windows — Reading
items.body:
Book pages: 4-6 · Day 1, Chapter 1 · CBO Objective: #1

Logging In to Windows

Most computer systems used in schools and businesses are networked, or connected. Keeping a network secure is an important part of making sure only authorized people can use it. Logging in to a computer is the process of entering your username and password to gain access to the computer and network.

Passwords

A strong password mixes uppercase, lowercase, numbers, and symbols — never a familiar name, birthday, or common word people could guess. Passwords should never be shared with anyone, including friends and family. Password managers such as 1Password, LastPass, RoboForm, or Avira can remember your passwords for you, so you only need to remember the one password for the manager itself.

What happens during the startup process?

From the moment you turn on the computer, the computer and Windows work together to get ready for you. Together they form the operating system — the collection of parts and pieces that we see and work with on the screen.

items.description:
Book pages: 4-6 · CBO Objective: #1

Hands-On 1.1: Log In to Windows

In this exercise, you will log in to your computer using the login name and password provided by your instructor.

  1. If necessary, turn on the computer and monitor. (The computer may already be switched on if you are in a computer lab.) Ask your instructor for help if necessary.
    After a pause, the computer begins starting up, which usually takes about a minute. When the startup process is complete, the lock screen appears.
  2. Click the lock screen to bring up the sign-in screen.
  3. Click the appropriate login from the lower-left corner of the screen. If you are the only person who uses your computer, your login may be the only one listed.
  4. Enter the password you were given into the blank password line and click the arrow button. This will take you to the Desktop.

What to submit

Once you're on the Desktop, open the Snipping Tool (Start → All Apps → Snipping Tool, or press Windows+Shift+S) and capture a screenshot of your Desktop right after signing in. Submit that screenshot as proof you logged in on your own.

criteria.description: Screenshot proves a successful, independent login

Partial Credit — screenshot shows progress (e.g. the lock/sign-in screen) but not a completed Desktop view
No Credit — no screenshot submitted, or it doesn't relate to the task

items.title: The Windows Desktop, Behind the Screen & Using a Mouse — Reading
items.body:
Book pages: 7-8 · Day 1, Chapter 1 · CBO Objective: #2

The Windows Desktop

Once you have logged in to the computer, you will be looking at the Windows Desktop. The Desktop is the primary work area in Windows, and like your desk at school, all the apps you are working with are placed on the computer.

The Desktop has many unique features that help you to be more efficient when using the computer: the Start button, icons, the background, program windows, program buttons, the computer and internet search box, the notification area, and the Show Desktop button.

{{img:pg 7.png|Textbook page 7 — the Windows Desktop}}

Book pages: 8-11 · Day 1, Chapter 1 · background knowledge, not a listed CBO objective

Behind the Screen: Basic Computer Components

Your computer is a collection of hardware parts working together with Windows and other software applications. Knowing the name and function of these components gives you a better understanding of the computing process. This section is background computer literacy — it isn't one of this chapter's five listed CBO competencies, but it supports understanding the Desktop and how the computer works.

Processor

The processor is often referred to as the "brain" of the computer. The central processing unit (CPU) does all the processing that keeps programs running, moves the cards when you play Solitaire, and does the math in your spreadsheet programs. How quickly these processes are carried out is largely determined by the gigahertz (GHz) rating of the CPU — a larger GHz rating means the processor can handle significantly more processing cycles per second.

Hard Drive

The hard drive is the permanent storage device in the computer — think of it as a large filing cabinet where all the files and programs that run on the computer are stored. Traditional hard drives use spinning magnetic platters; they're inexpensive and store huge amounts of data. Newer hard drives are solid state (SSDs) — no moving parts, much quicker to load data. The newest SSDs are very small and are generally called NAND SSDs.

Random Access Memory (RAM)

Hard drives operate at a relatively slow speed, so the computer does not run programs directly from the hard drive. When a program is used, it is first loaded into RAM to be accessed by the CPU. As you edit a letter or make a drawing, the information is being stored in RAM. RAM is considered temporary memory, though — unlike the hard drive, when the computer is turned off, all of the data in RAM is lost.

Universal Serial Bus (USB)

A USB port or connector is a small rectangular port that allows you to connect various pieces of equipment to your computer using a single standardized cord and plug. Before USB, different equipment had special connectors and cables, and it was much more difficult for new users to set up their computers.

Secure Digital (SD) Card

An SD card is a type of storage device typically found on digital cameras and other portable devices. Many desktop and laptop computers now come with an SD card reader built in. Some devices use micro SD cards, which are about the size of your thumbnail.

{{img:pg 8.png|Textbook page 8 — basic computer components}}

Book pages: 12-14 · Day 1, Chapter 1 · CBO Objective: #3

Using a Mouse

The mouse is your main tool for controlling programs on the Desktop. Moving the mouse with your hand controls the movements of the mouse pointer on the screen. With your mouse on a flat surface (a table or mouse pad), place your hand on the mouse so your index finger rests lightly on or above the left mouse button.

MotionNotes and How to Do It
PointHold the tip of the mouse pointer over an element on the screen. Keep the mouse steady.
Click (single-click)Used to "push" an onscreen button. Point to an onscreen element and push the left mouse button one time. Hold the mouse still and click gently.
DragUsed to move items around the screen, select text, and perform other tasks/commands. Point to an onscreen element, click and hold down the left mouse button, and move the onscreen element until it reaches the desired location. This is often called drag and drop.
Double-clickUsed to start a program or open a file/folder. Point to an onscreen element and quickly click the left mouse button twice. Hold the mouse still and click gently.
Right-clickUsed to display a pop-up menu of options that relate to the object. Point to an onscreen element and click the right mouse button once.
{{img:pg 12.png|Textbook page 12 — using a mouse}}

items.title: Passwords and Account Settings, Signing Out & Locking — Reading
items.body:
Book pages: 15 · Day 1, Chapter 1 · CBO Objective: #1 — account management extends the login competency

Passwords and Account Settings

All Windows users have their own login and password that allow them to connect to their various personal settings for the computer, as well as to other online accounts they may have that are connected to Windows.

Accessing Account Settings

The circular "person" icon of the individual logged in to the computer is located at the bottom of the Start menu. This user icon/name button gives you the option to change account settings when clicked: your login account, password, user account picture, and options for syncing your computer with other devices.

  • Sign-In Options: change your password and set whether your computer requires a password again after sleep mode.
  • Access Work or School: at work or school, you may be allowed to connect your personal computer to the network, if this is an option.
  • Other Users: on a home computer, if you have administrator privileges, you can add other users to the computer. The "Create One for a Child" button allows you to add users with specific privileges.
{{img:pg 15.png|Textbook page 15 — passwords and account settings}}

Book pages: 16-17 · Day 1, Chapter 1 · CBO Objective: #1 — session management extends the login competency; not separately listed in the CBO

Signing Out, Switching Users, and Locking the Computer

Signing out of the computer is different from turning off the computer. Before signing out, you need to save your files to the hard drive, because the computer closes the programs you were using and removes login information and settings from memory so it is ready for a new user to log on.

Multiple users can be signed on to a single computer at the same time. When you sign out, when you simply switch users, the previous user's information, screen settings, and programs are set aside in the computer's RAM instead — so that person's session can be quickly reimplemented if that person signs back in.

Locking the Computer

Locking the computer protects your PC from unauthorized use when you leave your desk. Locking causes the lock screen to display. To see your screen and continue working, you must re-enter your password.

TaskProcedure
Log off WindowsClick the Start button. Click your user icon/name button at the top of the menu and then click Sign Out.
Switch usersClick the Start button. Click your user icon/name button and then choose the desired user from the list.
Lock/Unlock WindowsClick your user icon/name button and choose Lock. This will lock the computer and show the lock screen. To unlock the computer, click the lock screen, click your user icon/name button, and enter your password when it appears.
{{img:pg 16.png|Textbook page 16 — signing out, switching users, and locking}}

items.title: The Start Menu — Reading
items.body:
Book pages: 18-20 · Day 2, Chapter 1 · CBO Objective: #4

The Start Menu

The Start menu is the one place you can go to launch most of the programs installed on your computer. Like all menus, the Start menu is a collection of commands, and these particular ones allow you to launch all of the programs that come with Windows. A command is a link that can launch (start or open) a file, folder, or app, or that can execute a variety of other tasks — you might compare a command to a light switch on a wall used to turn on a ceiling light.

The Start Menu Panes

The Start menu is divided into panes: the top pane shows a list of all pinned apps (you can add frequently used apps by pinning them to the Start menu), and the bottom pane lists recommended documents and apps — items you have recently used. The user icon/name button and Power options button are along the bottom of the menu.

items.title: The Pinned and Recommended Lists & Adding/Deleting Folders — Reading
items.body:
Book pages: 21-22 · Day 2, Chapter 1 · CBO Objective: #4

The Pinned and Recommended Lists

Windows 11 automatically adds commands for apps to the Pinned list in the Start menu. Sometimes an app is added to the list the first time you launch it; other times you may need to use a program twice to have it added to the list. When the Pinned list becomes full, the command for the app that has been unused the longest is removed. You can also add and delete apps to suit your needs. The Recommended section shows the documents and files you have opened most recently.

Pinning Commands to the Start Menu

Commands for any app can be easily pinned to the Start menu. You pin a command to the Start menu to make it easier to access.

{{img:pg 21.png|Textbook page 21 — the Pinned and Recommended lists}}

Moving Apps on the Start Menu

You can move apps around on the Start menu as you like, and you can move an app straight to the top of the menu by right-clicking the app icon with the mouse to open a menu of commands. If you have many apps, there may be more than one screen that you can scroll through on the Start menu.

Book pages: 22-24 · Day 2, Chapter 1 · CBO Objective: #4

Adding and Deleting Folders on the Start Menu

{{img:pg 22.png|Textbook page 22 — adding a folder to the Start menu}}

You can add folders to the Start menu to organize apps and shortcuts. When you drag one icon onto another icon on the Start menu, this triggers the creation of a folder. More icons can then be added to the folder by dragging and dropping icons onto the folder. Folder names can be renamed to help with organization — for example, one folder for social media apps, another for games, and another for apps you use for school.

Deleting a menu folder is easy. The selected folder is deleted once there is only one icon or shortcut left in the folder. At this point the last icon or shortcut is placed back on the Start menu and the folder is automatically deleted.

{{img:pg 24.png|Textbook page 24 — deleting a folder}}

items.title: Shutting Down — Reading
items.body:
Book pages: 24-26 · Day 2, Chapter 1 · CBO Objective: #5

Shutting Down

Windows is a very large collection of programs. If it is not shut down properly, you may discover upon restarting your computer that error messages appear — or even worse, that Windows won't start at all. This is because Windows needs time to properly shut down all of its software parts and pieces correctly, and turning off the power doesn't allow enough time to do this.

There are three ways to shut down Windows, depending on what you want to do next. The following options are displayed via the Start button and the Power button menu: Sleep, Shut Down, and Restart.

Sleep

In sleep mode, the computer slows down and therefore uses a lot less energy. Any documents you are working on are saved, the processor works more slowly, the monitor is turned off, and other settings are triggered that allow the computer to save power. On most laptops, closing the lid will immediately cause the laptop to go into sleep mode.

Shut Down

This command closes all programs, logs you out of the computer, and turns off its power. When you are done with the computer for the day, it is important to turn it off using the Shut Down command.

Never hold down the Power button to turn a computer off unless you have no other choice. Windows needs time to close its various parts and pieces down properly, and turning the power off abruptly can corrupt parts of the Windows software and can even cause the computer to not be able to restart.

Restart

The restart mode closes all open program windows, logs you out, and powers down the computer. The computer then restarts and Windows reloads. Sometimes Windows will ask you to restart the computer after a new program or program update has been installed, because the new program can't be used until the system restarts and the new software is integrated into Windows.

TaskProcedure
Shut down Windows and the computerClose all open programs. Click the Shut Down button (on the Power button menu).
Go into sleep modeChoose Sleep from the Power button menu.
Exit sleep modeMove the mouse or tap the Spacebar on your keyboard.

items.title: Hands-On 1.9: Sleep Mode and Shut Down
items.description:
Book pages: 24-26 · CBO Objective: #5

Hands-On 1.9: Sleep Mode and Shut Down

In this exercise, you'll put the computer into sleep mode, wake it back up, and then shut it down properly.

  1. Make sure all programs are closed and then click the Start button.
  2. Click the Power button, then choose Sleep from the menu.
  3. Move the mouse or press the Spacebar to bring the computer out of sleep mode.
  4. If the Start screen appears, click it. Enter your password when the login screen appears.
    The computer is now ready to work again.
  5. Make sure any open programs are closed.
  6. Click the Start button and then choose Power→Shut Down.
    It may take the computer 15 seconds or more to completely shut down.

About this deliverable: there's no way to submit a screenshot proving you shut the computer down — by definition, it's off. Do the steps above in class with your instructor watching, then take this 4-question quiz in place of a written submission. It checks that you know when to use Sleep vs. Shut Down vs. Restart, which is the real point of the exercise.

items.title: Controlling App Windows — Reading
items.body:
Book pages: 33-38 · Day 3, Chapter 2 · CBO Objective: #1

Controlling App Windows

Every app you open is displayed within its own app window. These windows have controls and features that are similar in most programs — learn how to use them in one app, and you can use them in almost any other.

Quick-Sizing Buttons

All apps use the same four quick-sizing buttons in the top-right corner of the window:

ButtonWhat It Does
MinimizeRemoves the app window from the screen but keeps it running, with its app button still on the taskbar
MaximizeEnlarges the app window to fill the screen
Restore DownResizes the app window back to the size it was before it was last maximized
CloseExits the app
{{img:pg 33.png|Textbook page 33 — quick-sizing buttons}}

Minimizing hides an app's clutter without closing it; maximizing simply covers the other open windows. Alt+F4 closes (exits) an app from the keyboard. A quick way to close a minimized app is to right-click its taskbar button and choose Close Window.

Moving and Resizing App Windows

The title bar at the top of a window can be dragged to move the window around the Desktop. You can resize a window by dragging any border or corner — if the mouse pointer doesn't turn into a double-headed arrow when you point at the border, the window can't be resized.

The Snap Feature

The Snap feature is another way to maximize, restore down, or view two windows side by side: drag a window's title bar to the top edge of the Desktop to maximize it, or to the left/right edge to fill half the screen.

{{img:pg 38.png|Textbook page 38 — resizing windows using Snap}}

Not every app window follows these standards exactly — some "nonstandard" windows are missing features or have them modified, either for appearance or because a feature isn't necessary for that app.

items.title: Hands-On 2.1-2.2: Use Quick-Sizing Buttons & Snap a Window
items.description:
Book pages: 35, 38 · CBO Objective: #1

Hands-On 2.1: Use Quick-Sizing Buttons

In this exercise, you will open File Explorer and use the quick-sizing buttons to maximize, restore down, and minimize the app window.

  1. Click the File Explorer button on the taskbar.
  2. If the app window does not fill the screen, click the Maximize button.
    The window enlarges to fill the entire Desktop, and the center button changes to Restore Down.
  3. Click the Restore Down button.
    The window returns to its original, smaller size.
  4. Click the Minimize button.
  5. Click the File Explorer button on the taskbar again to restore it to the Desktop.
  6. Click the Close button to exit File Explorer.

Hands-On 2.2: Move, Resize, and Snap a Window

In this exercise, you will move, resize, and snap the File Explorer app window.

  1. Click the File Explorer button on the taskbar. If necessary, restore down the app window.
  2. Click the title bar and drag the app window around the Desktop.
  3. Practice resizing the app window using its borders or corners.
  4. Drag the title bar to the left edge of the Desktop until the mouse pointer touches the edge.
    The window snaps to fill the left half of the screen.
  5. Repeat step 4 by dragging the window to the right edge, then the top edge.

What to submit

Once you've snapped File Explorer to one side of the screen (step 4), use the Snipping Tool to capture a screenshot and submit it.

criteria.description: Screenshot shows File Explorer snapped to one half of the screen

ratings.description: Full Credit — File Explorer clearly fills exactly half the screen (snapped, not just resized)

Book pages: 39-41 · Day 3, Chapter 2 · CBO Objective: #2

Touch Controls

Windows supports touch gestures on computers and devices with touchscreens, like tablets and smartphones. Using touch, you can move and control objects on the screen with one, two, or three fingers. If your laptop has a precision touchpad, many of the same gestures work there too.

Touch Gestures

TaskGesture
Open the Action CenterSwipe in from the right edge of the screen
Open Task ViewSwipe in from the left edge of the screen
View the title barSwipe down from the top of the screen
View the taskbarSwipe up from the bottom of the screen
Open, select, or activate an itemTap once on the item
Zoom in or outTouch with two or more fingers and drag them apart or together
{{img:pg 40.png|Textbook page 40 — touch gestures}}

Touchpad Controls

A laptop's touchpad can do more than just point and click. Three-finger swipes let you open Task View (swipe up), show the Desktop (swipe down), or switch between open windows (swipe right or left).

items.title: Working with the Taskbar — Reading
items.body:
Book pages: 41-43 · Day 3, Chapter 2 · CBO Objective: #3

Working with the Taskbar

The taskbar runs the width of the Desktop at the bottom of the screen. Icons for the Start menu and other default apps sit in the middle of the taskbar, along with buttons for any apps you have open.

Only one app window can be active at a time. The active app's button has a lighter, square background behind it; clicking an inactive app's button brings its window to the front and makes it active.

{{img:pg 41.png|Textbook page 41 — parts of the taskbar}}

Notification Area

The notification area on the right end of the taskbar has four jobs: it shows the system clock and date, shows icons for background tasks (like antivirus software), delivers notifications about system events, and gives quick access to certain apps.

Pinning and Unpinning Apps

You can pin app buttons to the taskbar so your most-used apps are always easy to find and launch, even when they're closed. A pinned app that isn't currently open won't have a square border around its icon. Right-click an app's icon to Pin to Taskbar or Unpin from Taskbar.

Hands-On 2.4: Change Taskbar Settings

  2. Right-click the Notepad app button on the taskbar and choose Pin to Taskbar.
  3. Right-click the Notepad app button again and choose Close All Windows.

Book pages: 44-47 · Day 3, Chapter 2 · CBO Objective: #5 and #6

Action Center (Notifications)

The Action Center is a central location for information shared by apps on your computer — everything from news alerts to Windows update notices. It's accessed by clicking the Notification button in the notification area (or pressing Windows+A), and it only appears when there are notifications to share.

Notifications

Notifications vary depending on the app. Hovering over a notification shows a Close button to dismiss just that item; clicking anywhere else on the screen closes the whole panel.

{{img:pg 45.png|Textbook page 45 — the Notifications panel}}

Actions

Below Notifications, the Action Center contains rows of actions — quick-access icons for settings like Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Airplane mode, Battery saver, Focus assist, and Accessibility, plus sliders for brightness and volume. The Edit Quick Settings button (the pencil icon) lets you show additional actions and customize which ones appear.

{{img:pg 47.png|Textbook page 47 — Action Center actions}}

items.title: Multitasking — Reading
items.body:
Book pages: 48-53 · Day 3, Chapter 2 · CBO Objective: #4

Multitasking

Multitasking is Windows' ability to run multiple programs or operations at the same time. Some multitasking happens in the background without you noticing — downloading updates, monitoring security — but you can also multitask on purpose: keep several programs open, check email, pay bills, and listen to music, all at once.

{{img:pg 48.png|Textbook page 48 — multitasking with multiple windows open}}

App Switching

You can work in only one app at a time — the active app. Windows places the active app's window in front of the others; its taskbar button is brighter, with a longer, lighter bar underneath it, while inactive buttons are darker with a short gray bar.

{{img:pg 49.png|Textbook page 49 — active vs. inactive app buttons}}

The Flip Command

The Flip command lets you quickly switch between open programs using the keyboard: hold Alt and tap Tab to display the Flip window, keep tapping Tab (while still holding Alt) until the app you want is selected, then release Alt.

Show Desktop and Task View

The Show Desktop button, at the far-right end of the taskbar, minimizes every open window at once so you can see the Desktop. The Task View button shows a screen with a live view of every open app, so you can switch to one with a single click instead of holding down keys.

items.description:
Book pages: 48-53 · CBO Objective: #4

Hands-On 2.7: Open Multiple Programs

In this exercise, you will open three programs from the Start menu and watch their app buttons get added to the taskbar.

  1. Click Start, then click Calculator (from the upper pane or All Apps).
  2. Open Notepad from All Apps.
  3. Open Paint from All Apps.
    There are now three app buttons on the taskbar. Leave all three programs open for the next exercises.

Hands-On 2.8: Switch Programs

In this exercise, you will change the active app by clicking inactive app buttons and windows on the taskbar.

  1. If Calculator is not the active app, click its taskbar button to make it active.
  2. Click a visible part of the Paint window (or its taskbar button) to make Paint active.
  3. Click the Maximize button to make Paint fill the Desktop.
  4. Although Paint is now hiding the other programs, click the Calculator app button on the taskbar to make it active again.
  5. Make Notepad active, then click its Close button to exit the app.
    Leave Calculator and Paint open.

Hands-On 2.9: Flip Between Active Programs

In this exercise, you will flip between your open apps using the keyboard.

  1. Start Notepad again so you have three apps open.
  2. Hold down the Alt key on the keyboard and keep it held down.
  3. While still holding Alt, tap the Tab key once.
    The Task-Switching box appears, showing icons for your open apps.
  4. While still holding Alt, keep tapping Tab until Calculator is selected in the Task-Switching box.
  5. Release Alt.
    Calculator becomes the active app and jumps to the front of the Desktop.
  6. Practice using Alt+Tab a few more times to switch between programs.

Hands-On 2.10: Use Task View

In this exercise, you will use the Task View button to switch between running apps.

  1. Click on the Paint app to make it active.
  2. Click the Task View button on the taskbar.
  3. Click Calculator in the Task View window.
    Calculator is now the active app on the Desktop.
  4. Practice using Task View to switch between your open apps, then close Calculator, Notepad, and Paint.

What to submit

Use the Snipping Tool to capture a screenshot of the Alt+Tab Task-Switching box while it's open (Hands-On 2.9, step 3 or 4), showing all of your open apps, then submit it.

Day 4 · Chapter 3 Reading

Book pages: 57-60 · CBO Objective: #1, #2, #3, #5

Why Online? The Cloud & Creating Your Microsoft Account

This chapter is shorter than the others — it exists purely to get you a free Microsoft account set up and connected to Windows, so every later chapter in this course can use it. There are no Skill Builder or Try This at Home exercises in this chapter.

Why Online?

The Internet has grown into a vast storage and access system — apps, documents, music, pictures, and video can now be accessed from any Internet-connected device, not just the one you created them on.

The Cloud

The cloud refers to storing apps and services on the Internet rather than only on your own computer, so they're accessible from anywhere. Many Windows 11 apps are already cloud-based. Popular cloud storage providers include Microsoft OneDrive, Dropbox, Google Drive, and box.

{{img:pg 59.png|Textbook page 59 — logos for four popular cloud storage sites}}

Microsoft 365 for the Web

Microsoft 365 for the web (sometimes called "Office for the web") is a free, browser-based version of Office — Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, OneDrive, Teams, and OneNote. It has basic functionality compared to the full paid desktop versions, but shares the same core features.

Creating Your Microsoft Account

If you already use Windows or another Microsoft service, you may already have a Microsoft account — use that one if so. Otherwise you'll create a new one in Hands-On 3.1.

Account Verification

After you sign up, Microsoft may send an email to verify your account. Clicking the verification link in that email unlocks all of your account's features.

Accounts and Apps

Account/AppWhat Is It For?
Windows loginSign on to the computer
Microsoft accountAllows access to OneDrive and Microsoft 365 for the web; needs to be connected with your Windows login
OneDriveMicrosoft's free online storage option and the starting point for accessing Microsoft 365 apps in this book

App Commands: Menus, Ribbons & the Quick Access Toolbar

Menu Commands

Older-style apps (like Notepad) use classic drop-down menus from a menu bar — File, Edit, Help, and so on. Menu names and commands vary from program to program, but many follow a similar convention.

{{img:pg 73.png|Textbook page 73 — Notepad's File drop-down menu}}

Commands in Programs with Ribbons

Since Office 2007, most Microsoft apps use a Ribbon instead of drop-down menus — a toolbar organized by task. Different apps' Ribbons (Paint's vs. Word's) share the same overall design even though their specific tools differ.

{{img:pg 75.png|Textbook page 75 — the Paint Ribbon compared to the Word Ribbon}}

Quick Access Toolbar

The Quick Access Toolbar sits above (or as part of) the Ribbon and defaults to three tools: Save, Undo, and Redo.

Ribbon Tabs

A Ribbon is organized into tabs (like Home, Insert, Layout), each containing command groups made up of buttons, drop-downs, and galleries. Hovering over any tool shows a ScreenTip naming it.

Book pages: 77-80 · CBO Objective: #5

Saving Your Work & Naming Files

Saving Your Work

Nothing is permanently saved until you tell the computer to save it. Saving to OneDrive means your work is accessible from anywhere.

Where Your Work Is Located

Until you save, your work sits in RAM — temporary memory that's cleared when the computer restarts or loses power.

Files and Folders

A file is a collection of data stored with a name; a folder stores a collection of files.

Choosing a Storage Location

You can save to your computer's internal hard drive (Notepad defaults to Documents, Paint defaults to Pictures), a portable USB flash drive, or OneDrive — OneDrive is the preferred method used throughout this book.

Filenames

RuleDetail
LengthUp to 255 characters
AllowedAll alphanumeric characters except the reserved ones below
Reserved characters| \ ? * < " : > /
Reserved wordsCON, PRN, AUX, NUL, COM1-9, LPT1-9
{{img:pg 79.png|Textbook page 79 — the Naming Files rules table}}

Save Versus Save As

Save As lets you save a copy of a file with a different name, in a different location, or in a different file format (like converting to PDF).

Mouse Pointers

PointerMeaning

TextI-beam, appears over editable text

Typing & Selecting Text in Word Online

The Word Ribbon

Word Online's Ribbon has tabs like Home and View. Drop-down lists (Font Name, Font Size, Font Color) show a ScreenTip when you hover, and the Ribbon can switch to a compact Simplified Ribbon Mode.

{{img:pg 91.png|Textbook page 91 — the blinking cursor (insertion point) versus the mouse pointer}}

The Cursor and the Mouse Pointer

These are two different things: the blinking cursor (insertion point) shows where typed text will appear, while the mouse pointer (often an I-beam over text) follows the mouse.

Special Keys

Backspace deletes the character before the cursor; Delete deletes the character after it. Tab indents. Enter ends a paragraph and moves the cursor down two lines; Shift+Enter moves down only one line without starting a new paragraph.

Editing and Selecting Text

Text must be selected before it can be edited or formatted.

MethodSelects
DragWhatever the mouse passes over
Double-clickOne whole word
Triple-clickOne whole paragraph
Ctrl+AThe entire document

Cut, Copy & Paste

CommandWhat It Does
CutRemoves the selected item and places a copy on the Clipboard
CopyLeaves the selected item in place and places a copy on the Clipboard
PasteInserts whatever is currently on the Clipboard
{{img:pg 100.png|Textbook page 100 — the Cut/Copy/Paste commands table}}

Keyboard Shortcuts

Ctrl+X (Cut), Ctrl+C (Copy), Ctrl+V (Paste). Some browser-based apps can't access the system Clipboard directly with the on-screen buttons — if a "Use shortcut keys" message appears, use the keyboard shortcuts instead.

{{img:pg 101.png|Textbook page 101 — the "Use shortcut keys" clipboard-access message}}

Advanced Cut, Copy, and Paste

Whatever you cut or copy stays on the Clipboard until you cut or copy something else, so you can paste the same item repeatedly — even into a different app than the one you copied it from.

Using Email

This chapter covers the Outlook Online app and the fundamentals of email: the parts of an inbox and a message, sending/receiving/replying, attaching files, organizing with folders, and protecting yourself from malicious email.

Learning objectives

  • Create a properly formatted email address
  • Send and receive emails, including those with attachments
  • Create folders and organize emails using Outlook
  • Identify spam and other email threats

What is email? The Outlook Online app (Hands-On 5.1-5.2)

You'll log in to Outlook via OneDrive (5.1) and read a message from the Outlook Team (5.2), getting familiar with the Outlook screen and its dynamic, responsive layout.

Sending, receiving, and replying (Hands-On 5.3-5.5)

Send a message (5.3), send one with an attachment (5.4), and reply to a message from your instructor (5.5). Every message needs an address line and message body — the subject line is technically optional but recommended.

Saving emails with folders (Hands-On 5.6-5.7)

Create folders to organize your Inbox (5.6), then move messages into them using both drag-and-drop and the Move To command (5.7).

Email safety (Hands-On 5.8)

Storing Files

This chapter is about organizing your digital life: creating folders and subfolders, moving/copying files, deleting and restoring them, and using OneDrive to store files in the cloud.

Learning objectives

  • Create new folders and subfolders for organizing your files
  • Move or copy folders and files from one location to another
  • Delete folders and files and, if necessary, restore them from the Recycle Bin
  • Use OneDrive to store your files and folders
  • Upload to and download from OneDrive

Creating folders (Hands-On 7.1-7.2)

Create a new folder on the Desktop (7.1) and on your flash drive (7.2). Folders can be nested inside other folders (subfolders) as many times as needed. Folder names can be up to 255 characters.

Moving and copying (Hands-On 7.3-7.5)

Practice the Cut/Copy/Paste method (7.3), drag-and-drop (7.4) — new users often find the right-click drag-and-drop easier, since it gives more control over what happens when you drop the file — and selecting multiple files at once (7.5).

Deleting and restoring (Hands-On 7.6)

Items deleted from an internal or external hard drive go to the Recycle Bin and can be restored; items deleted from a USB flash drive do NOT go to the Recycle Bin — they're gone.

OneDrive file storage (Hands-On 7.7-7.10)

Create a folder in OneDrive (7.7), navigate between folders (7.8), upload files to OneDrive (7.9), and download from OneDrive back to your computer (7.10).

Practice and assessment in this chapter

  • Complete a complicated search

Performing a basic web search (Hands-On 9.1-9.2)

Search engines index the web and match items to your keywords — they don't search the entire web instantly on demand. Being more specific in your search terms gets more relevant results. Practice a basic Google search (9.1) and a Google image search (9.2). Be aware of copyright when using images found online.

Defending yourself from web threats

A firewall checks data entering your computer and blocks anything that looks like a threat — Windows comes with one built in. Antivirus software needs to be updated regularly, since new viruses appear daily. On social media, remember that anything you post can stay on the Internet forever.

items.title: Chapter 10 Overview: Using Settings and Help
items.body:
Using Settings and Help

The final chapter: Windows Search, Settings (screen, power, updates), and the Store. Several exercises here use WebSims — since they involve system-level settings — via the Labyrinth Student Resource Center rather than direct hands-on practice in a shared lab computer.

Learning objectives

  • Search your computer using the new Search program
  • Change the screen resolution and Desktop background
  • Change the power options
  • Update Windows 11

Searching Windows and the web (Hands-On 10.1-10.3)

The Search box on the taskbar searches both your computer and the web at once. Practice a basic search (10.1), searching the web from Windows Search (10.2), and getting help for a specific app like File Explorer (10.3).

Using Settings (Hands-On 10.4-10.7, WebSims)

Settings has nine basic categories and covers most day-to-day configuration; the Control Panel still exists for legacy options. These four exercises use WebSims (browser-based simulations) since they touch system date/time, power, and update settings that shouldn't be changed on a shared lab computer: checking automatic date/time (10.4), power and battery options (10.5), the power plan (10.6), and Windows Update options (10.7).

Controlling the screen and the Store (Hands-On 10.8-10.9)

Higher screen resolution means more, smaller pixels. Browse the Microsoft Store's app categories (10.8) and use a WebSim to download the free Netflix app (10.9).

Practice and assessment in this chapter

  • Hands-On 10.1-10.9 — done together in class (10.4-10.7 and 10.9 via WebSim)
  • Skill Builder 10.1 (in-book: Change the Screen Resolution, WebSim) — independent practice, see the assignment in this module
  • Additional Skill Builders 10.1-10.2 (Change the Screen Background; Change an Accent Color — best done on your own PC, not the lab) — graded homework, see the assignments in this module
